answer:
Credit both — but not with the same relation, and not on the same event. The CRM has no single "author" property to argue over; it forces authorship apart into distinct events, each with its own actor, and once you do that the question mostly dissolves.

The decisive passage is the scope note of P94 has created, which draws exactly the line your cataloguer is drawing: "this is the composition of a poem, not its commitment to paper". P94 runs from an E65 Creation to the conceptual object it created, and the CRM says explicitly that it represents conceiving the intellectual content and "does not represent the act of creating the first physical carrier". So the CRM already separates composing a text from writing it out, and it names drafting as a paradigm case of E65 Creation ("the drafting of U.N. resolution 1441").

Recommended structure, per letter:

1. The sheet: an E22 Human-Made Object. It P128 carries the text, an E33 Linguistic Object. The handwriting and the letterhead are properties of the sheet, not of the text — keeping these two nodes apart is what lets you say the evidence bears on the hand and not (directly) on the composition.
2. The writing-out: an E12 Production, P108 has produced the E22. This is where the hand goes. P14 carried out by the clerk, P14.1 in the role of "scribe". The secretary attaches to the same event, P14 carried out by, P14.1 in the role of "signatory" — P14's scope note says "It implies causal or legal responsibility", which is precisely what a signature confers, and P14.1 "specifies the nature of an actor's participation". If you need the signing as a node in its own right (to date it, or to hang the signature on it as an E37 Mark), partition the production with P9 consists of into a writing sub-activity and a signing sub-activity; that event-partitioning pattern is the workaround the SIG reached for in t1345 when the same "in what capacity did this person act" problem came up, and it remains unresolved there.
3. The composing: a separate E65 Creation, P94 has created the E33. This is the only assertion that is genuinely in doubt.

So: the secretary is credited unambiguously and unconditionally, as signatory on the production — that is documented fact, not inference. The clerk is credited on the E65 Creation and as scribe on the production — and that is where the uncertainty lives. Do not let "creator" stay a single catalogue slot; the answer to "secretary or clerk" is that they occupied different positions in the CRM graph all along.

On the nameless clerk: create an E21 Person anyway. E21 comprises "real persons who live or are assumed to have lived", and the CRM's own Monotonicity discussion uses King Arthur to make the point that a contested individual should still be given an E21 node used "as the collection point for describing possible properties and existence of this individual". Give it an identifier of your own coinage (P1 is identified by an E41 Appellation such as "the Canal Company's junior clerk, hand A") and a P3 has note explaining that no name is attested. The alternative — attributing to the Canal Company as an E74 Group — throws away the very claim your cataloguer is making, namely that a distinct individual is behind the hand.

On recording the uncertainty, two layers, and they do different jobs:

Layer 1 (do this): an E13 Attribute Assignment for the contested attribution, rather than asserting P14 directly. P140 assigned attribute to the E65 Creation, P141 assigned the clerk, P177 assigned property of type "P14 carried out by", P14 carried out by your cataloguer, P4 has time-span the date of cataloguing, P16 used specific object the letters that were compared, P3 has note the handwriting-and-letterhead reasoning. This is the CRM's own documented practice: "statements of responsibility are expressed through knowledge creation events" such as E13, and the E13 scope note says the class "marks the fact that the maintaining team is in general neutral to the validity of the respective assertion, but registers someone else's opinion and how it came about". Crucially, this lets the original catalogue attribution to the secretary and your cataloguer's rival attribution to the clerk coexist as two E13s: the Monotonicity principle wants properties left unconstrained so that "conflicting instances of properties are merely accumulated".

Layer 2 (optional, and unsettled): if you want a graded value rather than just a named opinion, CRMinf is the family model for it. The cataloguer's reasoning is an I5 Inference Making (subclass of I1 Argumentation, of which E13 is also a subclass), J1 used as premise the belief about the handwriting, J2 concluded that an I2 Belief, whose J4 that points to an I4 Proposition Set holding "this E65 Creation was carried out by hand A", and whose J5 holds to be gives an I6 Belief Value — I6 requires at minimum TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN but explicitly admits probability or fuzziness. Be aware that this layer is not closed business: SIG Issue 349 Belief Values, opened from a request about "uncertain associations, such as \"probably author of\"" — your case, almost verbatim — is still Open, and has been taken up at five meetings without a general mechanism for attaching a certainty value to an ordinary property. So use I2/I6 if you need a machine-readable degree, but do not expect the wider CRM world to agree on how to read your numbers; the E13 layer is the interoperable part.

One caution about the evidence chain, which I think matters more than the class choices. The handwriting identifies the hand that formed the letters on the paper; that bears on the E12 Production, and it is comparatively strong. Composition is a further inference from penmanship, and it is weaker — a clerk may have penned a text the secretary dictated, in which case the secretary composed and the clerk merely wrote. Modelling these as two events lets you hold the strong claim and the weak claim at different confidences instead of collapsing both into one "attributed to" field. This is also why I did not reach for CRMtex TX2 Writing, which looks made for handwriting: TX2 is a subclass of LRMoo F28 Expression Creation, and F28 holds that the expression is created when it is captured on a carrier, so typing the penning as TX2 would silently assert that whoever held the pen created the text — the exact claim in dispute.

rejected_alternatives.why_not: The obvious class for the act of forming handwriting on a support, but it is a subclass of LRMoo F28 Expression Creation, whose scope note holds that an expression is created when captured on a carrier. Typing the clerk's penning as TX2 would therefore automatically assert that the clerk created the expression — precisely the proposition we are uncertain about. E12 Production of the sheet asserts only that he made the object.

Same reason at the parent level: F28 fuses the conceptual creation and the making of the first carrier into one event (it is a subclass of both E12 and E65). That fusion is convenient for ordinary authorship and fatal here, because the whole case is that composing and inscribing may have been done by different people.

Technically safe — the letter issued in the company's name — but it discards the cataloguer's finding. Attributing to the corporate body would be the right retreat only if the evidence pointed to no individual at all; t1477 raises exactly this ambiguity in what P14 means when a Group carries out an activity, and it is unresolved.

rejected_alternatives.option: E31 Document for the letters' content
rejected_alternatives.why_not: A letter arguing a toll-rights case does make propositions about reality, so E31 is arguable, and multiple instantiation would allow both. But E33 Linguistic Object is what P94 has created and P128 carries need, and it is what carries P72 has language; nothing in this case turns on the propositional-truth aspect that E31 adds.

rejected_alternatives.option: E79 Part Addition for the signing
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Reads as though the signature were a physical part added to the letter. E79 requires an instance of E18 Physical Thing to be added; ink forming a name is not a separable physical part.

rejected_alternatives.option: E17 Type Assignment for the attribution
rejected_alternatives.why_not: A subclass of E13 restricted to classifying an item under an E55 Type via P42. Attributing an actor to an event is not a classification; the general E13 with P177 assigned property of type is what the CRM offers for asserting an arbitrary property.

rejected_alternatives.option: Asserting P14 carried out by directly from the E65 Creation to the clerk
rejected_alternatives.why_not: This states as fact what the CRM's own Authorship of Knowledge Base Contents principle says is read as the maintaining institution's official view. Given no corroborating record of the clerk anywhere in the collection, the honest record is an E13 naming the cataloguer as the source of the claim.

rejected_alternatives.option: Leaving the clerk out and recording the doubt in free text
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Legitimate if the doubt is never to be queried — the E13 scope note itself says whether such assignments need explicit structure depends on whether the information should be accessible by structured queries. But it makes the hypothesis invisible to any search for the clerk's hand across the collection, which is the one use the cataloguer plainly has in mind.

siblings_considered.why_not: E78 Curated Holding fits the bundle as an aggregation assembled and maintained by the archive, and you may well want one for the bundle. It is wrong for the individual letters, which are single physical objects; the handwriting and letterhead evidence attaches to each sheet, not to the aggregation.

E31 Document covers immaterial items making propositions about reality, which these letters do. But the case turns on the letters as expressions in natural language whose composition is at issue — E33 is what P94 has created reaches and what P128 carries links to the sheet. E31 adds a truth-claim dimension nothing here depends on.

E79 Part Addition would treat the secretary's signature as a part being added to the letter. A signature is not an instance of E18 Physical Thing being added; the finished, signed letter is better documented as one E12 Production with two participants distinguished by P14.1 in the role of.

E11 Modification is the other obvious event class for 'someone did something that resulted in this letter'. But E11 is about altering an instance of E24 Physical Human-Made Thing; using it for the drafting would anchor the composing to the paper and collapse exactly the text/carrier distinction that P94's scope note insists on.

E74 Group is the live rival: credit the Canal Company rather than a person nobody can name. Rejected because the cataloguer's claim is specifically that one individual hand drafted these letters; an E21 node with no attested name still holds that claim, and E21 explicitly covers persons 'assumed to have lived'.

E87 Curation Activity genuinely describes what the cataloguer is doing, and could be recorded alongside. It is the wrong carrier for the claim itself: E87 relates to an E78 Curated Holding via P147 curated and has no way to say which property was asserted to hold between which two things. Only E13 carries P140/P141/P177.

I7 Belief Adoption covers taking over propositions from a source you trust, as in citing a paper. The cataloguer is not adopting anyone's stated belief — there is no other record of the clerk — but inferring from physical evidence, which is what I5 Inference Making is for.

I2's only siblings under E2 Temporal Entity are E3 Condition State and E4 Period, and neither is a plausible rival — E3 is the physical condition of an object over a time-span. I am naming the closest as the rule allows; there is no real competitor to I2 Belief for holding a graded truth value.

notes: The system put the decisive text in front of me only late and by accident: the P94 has created scope note ("the composition of a poem, not its commitment to paper") settles the composed-versus-signed question outright, but no search for uncertainty, authorship or attribution surfaced it — I found it only by running concept P94 to check a property I had already decided to use. concept E65 does not quote its own P94 scope note, so a reader who stops at the class dossier misses it. Similarly, concept on an extension class (I2, I5, F28, TX2) prints no siblings block at all, even when the parent is CRMbase (I2 is a subclass of E2, whose CRMbase siblings E3 and E4 the tool will happily list in the other direction from concept E3). That made the sibling entries for the two CRMinf classes guesswork about what the checker considers a sibling. Also, section paths such as "Modelling principles > Authorship of Knowledge Base Contents" are printed as the citable handle by docs but are rejected by quote; --json is needed to recover the real chunk ids (crm732#s0046 etc.), which is not documented in the brief. One substantive gap I could not close: I found no SIG discussion of the specific amanuensis case (dictation, or a clerk drafting for a signing superior) despite several searches; the nearest live discussions are t1345 on acting on behalf of an organisation and t1477 on what P14 means for a Group, both unresolved, and Issue 349 on belief values, still Open after five meetings.
